rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report says Muhammad came by God's command with religious and worldly good; if Quraysh refused, he would wait for God's judgment. They demanded a spring and garden, and he said such demands belonged to God, not his obligation.
rows.anchor: فإن سمعتم وأطعتم فحسن، وإلا صبرت لأمر الله حتى يحكم الله

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read the verb passively, with al-samāʾ accusative: the sky is made to fall.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور «أو تسقط» بضم التاء، «السماء» نصب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads al-samāʾ nominative as subject of an active verb: the sky falls.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد «أو تسقط السماء» برفع «السماء» وإسناد الفعل إليها

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They leave the sīn of kasfan unvowelled except in al-Rūm, where it is vowelled; the word means fragments.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي «كسفا» بسكون السين إلا في الروم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets kasfan as the whole sky; the author notes kasafa is used for cutting cloth.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: السماء جميعا وتقول العرب: كسفت الثوب ونحوه قطعته

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives kasf from covering and reads the phrase as the sky falling in pieces.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: المعنى أو تسقط السماء علينا قطعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects deriving kasf from covering as unattested in lexical sources; he derives it from cutting and explains eclipses as a cutting-away.
rows.anchor: وليس بمعروف في دواوين اللغة كسف بمعنى غطى، وإنما هو بمعنى قطع

rows.speaker: نافع وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر
rows.claim: They read kasfan with fatḥa on sīn, meaning pieces as the plural of kasfa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر «كسفا» بفتح السين أي قطعا جمع كسفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qabīlan can mean visibly face-to-face, a guarantor who confirms the Prophet, or a kind unlike what people know; al-Aʿraj reads qibalan.
rows.anchor: وقوله قبيلا قيل معناه مقابلة وعيانا

rows.speaker: قال المفسرون
rows.claim: Zukhruf here means gold, but more generally it is any ornament; the usage is linked to earth's adornment in 10:24.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: «الزخرف» الذهب في هذا الموضع، والزخرف ما تزين به

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd's reading glosses zukhruf as gold; Mujahid says the word became known through that reading.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد ما كنا نعرف الزخرف حتى قرأنا في حرف عبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In heaven” may mean high in the air, since Arabs call elevated air heaven; more apparently, the known heaven is meant, where God is and whose news reaches the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والعرب تسمي الهواء علوا سماء لأنه في حيز السمو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tarquā means to ascend; ruqiyy means ascent.
rows.anchor: وترقى معناه تصعد، والرقي الصعود

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي أمية
rows.claim: A report identifies Ibn Abī Umayya as the speaker who would not believe until Muhammad descended with a letter from God addressed to him.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن قائل هذه المقالة هو عبد الله بن أبي أمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply glorifies God as exempt from bringing angels or a book as demanded, or from the Prophet proposing such wonders; his duty is only to convey the law.
rows.anchor: أي تنزيها له من الإتيان مع الملائكة قبيلا، ومن أن يخاطبكم بكتاب كما أردتم

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وابن عامر
rows.claim: They read “He said, Glory be to my Lord,” reporting the Prophet's glorification in response.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وابن عامر «قال سبحان ربي» على معنى الخبر عن رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question reproaches people with astonishment: after guidance came, only a flimsy pretext and groundless rejection kept them from belief.
rows.anchor: إلا هذه العلة النزرة والاستبعاد الذي لا يستند إلى حجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sending humans as messengers is neither novel nor strange; humans can understand and reflect through a messenger of their own kind.
rows.anchor: وبعثة البشر رسلا غير بدع ولا غريب، فيها يقع الإفهام والتمكن من النظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If settled inhabitants of earth were angels, God would send an angel suited to them; humans would recoil from an angel and their eyes and hearts could not bear it.
rows.anchor: وأما البشر فلو بعث إليهم ملك لنفرت طباعهم من رؤيته

rows.speaker: البخاري
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī reports that Quraysh ended their demands by asking for angels to accompany Muhammad and testify to his prophethood.
rows.anchor: روى البخاري أن الملأ من قريش الذين قالوا لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī reports Quraysh asked Muhammad, “Who will testify for you?”
rows.anchor: قال المهدوي: روي أنهم قالوا له: فمن يشهد لك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though Quraysh did not explicitly name the witness, their point was to demand testimony; God witnesses and knows the truthful and liar.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أقوالهم إنما هو طلب شهادة دون أن يذكروها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God creates guidance and misguidance in human hearts; Muhammad's role is only to convey the message.
rows.anchor: ثم رد الأمر إلى خلق الله تعالى واختراعه الهدى والضلال في قلوب البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that the misguided find no allies besides God is a threat.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله فلن تجد لهم أولياء من دونه وعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes blindness, muteness, and deafness figuratively for confusion and anguish, or inability to see or hear what pleases them or present an argument.
rows.anchor: فقيل هي استعارات إما لأنهم من الحيرة والهم والذهول يشبهون أصحاب هذه الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the conditions literally at resurrection; God restores sight, hearing, and speech, so they see the Fire and hear its roar.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي حقيقة كلها، وذلك عند قيامهم من قبورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal view says God enables movement on their faces as he enabled movement on their feet in this world.
rows.anchor: أقدرهم الله على النقلة على الوجوه، كما أقدر في الدنيا

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: When asked how an unbeliever walks on his face, the Prophet says the One who made him walk on two feet in this world can make him walk on his face in the next; Qatāda affirms this.
rows.anchor: الآخرة على وجهه» ؟ قال قتادة: بلى وعزة ربنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the flame subsides after burning them and then flares; the increased blaze is in their punishment, while Hell itself never weakens.
rows.anchor: فالزيادة في حيزهم، وأما جهنم فعلى حالها من الشدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khabat means the flame subsides while embers remain; khamad means embers weaken; hamadat means the fire is extinguished altogether.
rows.anchor: وخبت النار معناه سكن اللهيب والجمر على حاله، وخمدت معناه سكن الجمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line describes a fire that does not go out before dawn and is covered with wet sandalwood when its flame subsides.
rows.anchor: أمن زينب ذي النار قبيل الصبح ما تخبو

rows.speaker: عدي بن زيد
rows.claim: ʿAdī ibn Zayd's verse illustrates a flame that alternately dies down and flares.
rows.anchor: طوراً تخبو وطورا تثير

rows.speaker: القطامي
rows.claim: Al-Qaṭāmī uses khabā for a fire that subsides briefly and then blazes again.
rows.anchor: فتخبو ساعة وتهب ساعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That is their recompense” points to the preceding threat of Hell.
rows.anchor: الإشارة إلى الوعيد المتقدم بجهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's signs include Muhammad's proofs and the Qur'an, its reports, commands, and prohibitions; resurrection is singled out to stress the gravity of denying it.
rows.anchor: بآياتنا يعم الدلائل والحجج التي جاء بها محمد عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rufāt is what decay reduced to dust; baʿth is movement of something still.
rows.anchor: و «الرفات» بقية الشيء التي قد أصارها البلى إلى حال التراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their question about being raised again expresses denial and, in their view, implausibility.
rows.anchor: وهذا الاستفهام منهم هو على جهة الإنكار والاستبعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who accept God originated the heavens, earth, and humans must admit he can recreate humans; the Messenger's proofs show this possible act will occur.
rows.anchor: فكيف يصح لهم أن يقروا بخلقه للكل وإخراجه من خمول العدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruʾya here is inward perception, the vision of the heart.
rows.anchor: و «الرؤية» في هذه الآية رؤية القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed term may mean the Resurrection or time of death; on the latter reading, singular stands generically for plural.
rows.anchor: و «الأجل» هنا يحتمل أن يريد به القيامة ويحتمل أن يريد أجل الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument establishes God's power and sovereignty over creation, strengthening the case for resurrection whenever he wills.
rows.anchor: ومقصد هذا الكلام بيان قدرة الله عز وجل وملكه لخلقه

rows.speaker: المتأولون والرواة
rows.claim: Exegetes and transmitters agree five signs were plague, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood, the signs in 7:133.
rows.anchor: اتفق المتأولون والرواة أن الآيات الخمس التي في سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās names hand, tongue after its knot was loosened, staff, and sea.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: هي يده ولسانه حين انحلت عقدته

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī names sea, staff, blight, and stone; he says God turned Pharaoh's wealth to stone and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz saw remnants.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن كعب القرطبي: هي البحر والعصا والطمسة والحجر

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk counts two staff signs separately, along with the hand and Moses' tongue-knot.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: هي إلقاء العصا مرتين، واليد، وعقدة لسانه

rows.speaker: عكرمة ومطر الوراق والشعبي
rows.claim: They name staff, hand, years of scarcity, and reduced produce.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة ومطر الوراق، والشعبي: هي العصا واليد والسنون

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan counts the staff becoming a serpent and swallowing the magicians' fabrications as signs.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هي العصا في كونها ثعبانا وتلقف العصا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another Ibn ʿAbbās report names scarcity in the countryside, reduced fruits in towns, hand, and staff.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هي السنون في بواديهم، ونقص الثمرات في قراهم

rows.speaker: مطرف عن مالك
rows.claim: Mālik's list, transmitted by Muṭarrif, is staff, hand, mountain, and sea; Ibn Wahb says Mālik substituted stone for sea.
rows.anchor: وروى مطرف عن مالك أنها العصا، واليد، والجبل إذ نتق، والبحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse singles out nine of Moses' many signs, more than twenty-four, calls them clear, and does not identify them; scholars rely on inference or reports.
rows.anchor: والذي يلزم من الآية أن الله تعالى خص من آيات موسى إذ هي كثيرة جدا

rows.speaker: صفوان بن عسال
rows.claim: A report says Moses' signs were commandments: avoid idolatry, theft, adultery, murder, false accusation, sorcery, usury, slander, fleeing battle, and Sabbath violation.
rows.anchor: هن أن لا تشركوا بالله شيئا

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reports fasal instead of fasʾal, following a dialect that says saʾala-yasʾalu.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الكسائي «فسل» على لغة من قال سأل يسأل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ask may address Muhammad's contemporaries about unseen details, or earlier Israelites who met Moses; on the second reading, examine their history and scriptures, as in 43:45.
rows.anchor: أي اسأل معاصريك عما أعلمناك به من غيب القصة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says asking means examining the Qur'an itself.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: سؤالك نظرك في القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās' reading is understood as Moses asking Pharaoh to release Israelites from torment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس «فسأل بني إسرائيل» أي فسأل موسى فرعون

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group takes masḥūran literally as passive: Moses was bewitched, so his speech and message were unsound.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة هو مفعول على بابه، أي إنك قد سحرت

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī interprets masḥūran as active, like mastūr, mashʾūm, and maymūn.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: هو مفعول بمعنى فاعل كما قال حجابا مستورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active derivation works only as “possessor of sorcery”; literal passive is a sound insult, while active sense conflicts with Pharaoh's reported “O magician,” unless speakers or attitudes shifted.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يتخرج إلا على النسب أي ذا سحر ملكته وعلمته

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب وغيره
rows.claim: ʿAlī and others read ʿalimtu in first person: Pharaoh never knew, while Moses did; al-Kisāʾī also reads this way.
rows.anchor: روي عن علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه وغيره أنه قرأ «علمت»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person reading suits literal masḥūran: Moses replies he knows God's signs and is sound in mind.
rows.anchor: فلما رماه فرعون بأنه قد سحر ففسد نظره وعقله وكلامه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read ʿalimta in second person, accusing Pharaoh of knowing denial; some cite deliberate unbelief as in 27:14.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «لقد علمت» بتاء المخاطب مفتوحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open-ta reading may reproach Pharaoh as plainly able to know, not report inner knowledge.
rows.anchor: أي أنت بحال من يعلم هذا، وهي من الوضوح بحيث تعلمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “These” refers to the nine signs.
rows.anchor: والإشارة ب هؤلاء إلى التسع الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baṣāʾir is plural of baṣīra, guiding paths and metaphorically the mind's path in judgment and belief; it is circumstantial accusative.
rows.anchor: وقوله بصائر جمع بصيرة، وهي الطريقة أي طرائق يهتدى بها

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن عباس والضحاك وابن زيد
rows.claim: Mathbūr means destroyed for Mujāhid, overcome for Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, deranged for Ibn Zayd, and accursed in another report.
rows.anchor: و «المثبور» المهلك، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say Moses, strengthened by prophethood after fear and gentle instruction, judged harshly on his own; others say he exceeded God's command or would not curse.
rows.anchor: كان موسى عليه السلام في أول أمره يجزع، ويؤمر بالقول اللين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istafazzah means make people flee or dislodge them by killing or expulsion; the land here is Egypt, read in context.
rows.anchor: يستفزهم معناه يستخفهم ويقلعهم، إما بقتل أو بإجلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage compresses Moses' story: Pharaoh sought to overpower and kill Israelites, but God drowned him and his soldiers.
rows.anchor: أراد فرعون غلبتهم وقتلهم وهذا كان بدء الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Pharaoh drowned, Israelites were told to settle in Syria; the promised latter event is Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر تعالى أمر «بني إسرائيل» بعد إغراق فرعون بسكنى أرض الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lafīfan means a mixed gathering brought together without tribal division or separation.
rows.anchor: و «اللفيف» الجمع المختلط الذي قد لف بعضه إلى بعض

rows.speaker: بعض اللغويين والطبري
rows.claim: Some linguists call lafīf a collective plural with no same-form singular; al-Ṭabarī takes it as a verbal noun, which the author questions.
rows.anchor: قال بعض اللغويين: هو من أسماء الجموع ولا واحد له من لفظه

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبعرى
rows.claim: The poem's word mathbūr describes one who follows Satan in the path of error and turns with him.
rows.anchor: إذا جاري الشيطان في سنن الغ ... ي ومن مال ميله مثبورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “We sent it down” refers to Qur'an in 17:89 or the familiar Qur'an in a fresh statement, as in 38:32.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قوله أنزلناه عائد على القرآن المذكور

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrāwī says the Qur'an was sent rightly for people's benefit and descended with truth in commands, prohibitions, and reports.
rows.anchor: قال الزهراوي: معناه بالواجب الذي هو المصلحة والسداد للناس

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī treats the two truth statements as equivalent: the Qur'an's reports and commands are true.
rows.anchor: وذهب الطبري إلى أنهما بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh parses qurʾānan as governed by an omitted verb explained by the next: “We divided a Qur'an.”
rows.anchor: مذهب سيبويه أن نصبه بفعل مضمر يفسره الظاهر بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, qurʾānan can be coordinated with pronoun in arsalanāka because sending and revealing serve one purpose.
rows.anchor: ويصح أن يكون معطوفا على الكاف في أرسلناك

rows.speaker: جمهور من الناس
rows.claim: The majority read farraqnāhu lightly, meaning clarified, distinguished, or made a criterion.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور من الناس «فرقناه» بتخفيف الراء، ومعناه بيناه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو رجاء وعلي بن أبي طالب وابن مسعود وأبي بن كعب والشعبي وحميد وعمرو بن فائد
rows.claim: They read farraqnāhu with doubled rāʾ; Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy add “to him,” emphasizing portions, matching measured recitation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو رجاء وعلي بن أبي طالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual revelation followed events over time; estimates are 25, 23 from Ibn ʿAbbās, 20 from Qatāda, and 18 attributed to al-Ḥasan, which is called unsound.
rows.anchor: فَقيل: في خمس وعشرين سنة، وقال ابن عباس: في ثلاث وعشرين سنة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن عباس وابن جريج وابن زيد
rows.claim: They take “at a measured pace” to mean deliberate recitation or tartīl.
rows.anchor: هذا قول مجاهد وابن عباس وابن جريج وابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation is a long span, with revelation coming portion by portion.
rows.anchor: والتأويل الآخر أي على مكث وتطاول في المدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal noun tanzīlan intensifies the preceding sense; readers agree on ḍamma on mīm of makth, though Arabic has other forms.
rows.anchor: وقوله ونزلناه تنزيلا مبالغة وتأكيد بالمصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Believe or do not” belittles unbelievers and threatens them: belief or disbelief harms themselves; the learned are the proof.
rows.anchor: تحقير للكفار، وفي ضمنه ضرب من التوعد

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One view identifies those given prior knowledge as believers among the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة: هم مؤمنو أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another view identifies them as Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, and similar figures.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: هم ورقة بن نوفل وزيد بن عمرو بن نفيل

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A report says scriptural scholars recognized the promised Prophet's description in Torah, praised God, and leaned toward Islam; the verse was revealed about them.
rows.anchor: وهذه صفته، ووعد الله به واقع لا محالة وجنحوا إلى الإسلام

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another view identifies the learned one as Muhammad; “before it” refers to Qur'an, as does “in it.”
rows.anchor: والضمير في قبله عائد على القرآن حسب الضمير في به

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another view takes both pronouns to refer to Muhammad and introduces Qur'an separately with “when recited.”
rows.anchor: وقيل الضميران لمحمد. واستأنف ذكر القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lil-adqān means toward their side; Ibn ʿAbbās says faces, al-Ḥasan says chin, the lower face nearest ground in prostration.
rows.anchor: وعليهما قال ابن عباس: المعنى للوجوه

rows.speaker: سيبويه والفراء
rows.claim: Sībawayh reads in as light emphatic with emphatic lām; al-Farrāʾ reads negation with lām meaning “except.”
rows.anchor: هي عند سيبويه المخففة من الثقيلة، واللام بعدها لام التوكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “believe or do not” directly threatens that they will see recompense, unlike earlier scriptural communities who humbled themselves.
rows.anchor: ويتوجه في هذه الآية معنى آخر وهو أن يكون قوله آمنوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse intensifies praise of the learned and urges anyone with knowledge to reach this rank.
rows.anchor: هذه مبالغة في صفتهم ومدح لهم وحض لكل من ترسم بالعلم

rows.speaker: التميمي
rows.claim: Al-Tamīmī says knowledge that does not make its recipient weep is unlikely to be beneficial.
rows.anchor: إن من أوتي من العلم ما لم يبكه لخليق أن لا يكون أوتي علما ينفعه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says polytheists heard Muhammad invoke Allah and al-Raḥmān and objected that he had ordered one god but prayed to two.
rows.anchor: سبب نزول هذه الآية أن المشركين سمعوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: مكحول
rows.claim: Makḥūl says a polytheist heard the Prophet invoke al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm, mistook the name for a man in Yamāma, prompting the clarification.
rows.anchor: وقال مكحول: تهجد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ليلة

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa reads ayyan mā tadʿū fa-lahu al-asmāʾ, meaning God has all other beautiful names.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة بن مصرف «أيا ما تدعوا فله الأسماء»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names express best attributes and require revealed authorization, not independent reasoning; a report lists ninety-nine names.
rows.anchor: وهي بتوقيف، لا يصح وضع اسم الله بنظر إلا بتوقيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whichever name one invokes, it is the one God who possesses all beautiful names.
rows.anchor: أي الأسماء تدعوا به فأنت مصيب له الأسماء الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Absolute whispering is inaudible even to speaker, but here the command means lowering the voice without total silence.
rows.anchor: هذه هي حقيقته، ولكنه في الآية عبارة عن خفض الصوت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعائشة وجماعة
rows.claim: They understand ṣalāt as supplication.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس وعائشة وجماعة: هي الدعاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also takes ṣalāt as Qur'an recitation in prayer; loud recitation brought abuse, so the Prophet was told to use moderate volume audible to companions but not provoking polytheists.
rows.anchor: والسبب أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم جهر بالقرآن فسمعه المشركون

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sīrīn says the verse was revealed about Bedouins reciting tashahhud aloud.
rows.anchor: قال ابن سيرين: كان الأعراب يجهرون بتشهدهم، فنزلت الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Bakr recited quietly to privately supplicate; ʿUmar aloud to repel Satan and wake sleepers. Later Abū Bakr was told to raise his voice and ʿUmar lower his.
rows.anchor: فلما نزلت هذه الآية، قيل لأبي بكر: ارفع أنت قليلا

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha also takes ṣalāt to mean tashahhud.
rows.anchor: الصلاة» يراد بها في هذه الآية التشهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: They say not to overdo loudness or ruin prayer by whispering, but to follow a middle way.
rows.anchor: ولا تحسن صلاتك في الجهر ولا تسئها في السر

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the verse rejects alternating loud and quiet practices of Gospel and Torah communities.
rows.anchor: النهي عما يفعله أهل الإنجيل والتوراة من رفع الصوت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report says do not recite aloud in daytime prayers or whisper in night prayers, but follow the prescribed way.
rows.anchor: ولا تجهر بصلاة النهار ولا تخافت بصلاة الليل

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says one who can make his ears hear has not whispered; the author calls it the basic linguistic sense, though the Abū Bakr report complicates it.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن مسعود لم يخافت من أسمع أذنيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes Jews, Christians, and Arabs who claimed ʿUzayr, Jesus, or angels were God's offspring, and rebuts Arabs who said God would be humiliated without allies.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية رادة على اليهود والنصارى والعرب في قولهم أفذاذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Negating a protector “from humiliation” denies need born of weakness; God's alliance with righteous servants is grace and mercy.
rows.anchor: إذ ولايته موجودة بتفضله ورحمته لمن والى من صالحي عباده

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says God did not ally with anyone or seek anyone's help.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: المعنى لم يحالف أحدا ولا ابتغى نصر أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takbīran is the Arabs' strongest expression of reverence, reinforced by the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: أبلغ لفظة للعرب في معنى التعظيم والإجلال، ثم أكدها بالمصدر

rows.speaker: مطرف عن عبد الله بن كعب
rows.claim: A report says the Torah opened with Sūrat al-Anʿām and ended with this sūra's close.
rows.anchor: وروى مطرف عن عبد الله بن كعب قال: افتتحت التوراة

rows.speaker: جميع المفسرين
rows.claim: All commentators say the sūra is Meccan; a minority says its opening through 18:8 came in Medina, but the author prefers the first view.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية في قول جميع المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra is among the Qur'an's most excellent chapters.
rows.anchor: وهي من أفضل سور القرآن

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Reports attribute great merit: Friday recitation brings forgiveness to the next Friday plus three days; another promises light and protection from the grave's trial.
rows.anchor: من قرأ بها يوم الجمعة غفر له ما بينه وبين الجمعة الأخرى

rows.speaker: حفص عن عاصم
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim pauses slightly after ʿiwajā and after marqadnā in 36:52.
rows.anchor: كان حفص عن عاصم يسكت عند قوله عوجا سكتة خفيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews prompted Quraysh to ask about spirit, cave youths, and Dhu al-Qarnayn. Muhammad promised next-day answers without “if God wills”; revelation paused fifteen days, prompting rumors his jinn companion abandoned him or he ran out of fabrications.
rows.anchor: لما سألته قريش عن المسائل الثلاث، الروح، والكهف، وذي القرنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When revelation resumed, opening praise of God for sending the Book rebuked Quraysh, who wished him ill but saw blessing on him.
rows.anchor: فافتتح الوحي بحمد الله الذي أنزل على عبده الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is the Qur'an; “no crookedness” means it was not diverted from the upright course.
rows.anchor: والكتاب هو القرآن، وقوله ولم يجعل له عوجا أي لم يزله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic ʿiwaj with kasra describes abstractions and roads; ʿawaj with fatḥa describes physical things like sticks and walls.
rows.anchor: وهو بكسر العين في الأمور والطرق وما لا يحس متنصبا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the phrase as meaning the Qur'an was not created.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: معناه ولم يجعله مخلوقا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh takes qayyiman as circumstantial accusative from “the Book,” advanced semantically but delayed in wording, interrupted by “no crookedness.”
rows.anchor: وقوله قيما نصب على الحال من الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, qayyiman is governed by an omitted verb; Companion codices add “but made it upright,” as Qatāda reports.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض مصاحف الصحابة «ولم يجعل له عوجا لكن جعله قيما»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk gloss qayyim as straight.
rows.anchor: ومعنى «قيم» مستقيم، هذا قول ابن عباس والضحاك

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī says the Qur'an confirms other scriptures; the author allows this but says it does not mean straight.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه أنه قيم على سائر الكتب بتصديقها، ذكره المهدوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another sense is that the Qur'an administers God's charge over the world, supported by universal warning and glad tidings.
rows.anchor: ويصح أن يكون معنى «قيم» قيامه بأمر الله عز وجل على العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Severe punishment is afterlife punishment, possibly worldly punishment like Badr; it is the second object of the warning verb.
rows.anchor: و «البأس الشديد» عذاب الآخرة، ويحتمل أن يندرج معه في النذارة عذاب الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min ladunhu means from God or his presence, and the pronoun refers to God.
rows.anchor: وقوله من لدنه أي من عنده ومن قبله

rows.speaker: الجمهور وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر
rows.claim: The majority read min ladunhu with ḍamma on dāl; Abū Bakr's ʿĀṣim reading has still dāl and kasra on nūn and hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور من «لدنه» بضم الدال وسكون النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ladun has forms and drops nūn in annexation; reward is Paradise preceded by worldly good, makithīn is circumstantial, abadan marks endless time.
rows.anchor: وفي «لدن» لغات، يقال «لدن» مثل سبع

rows.speaker: عبد الله وطلحة
rows.claim: They read yubashshiru with fatḥa on yāʾ, still bāʾ, and ḍamma on shīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وطلحة «ويبشر» بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq transmits Quraysh sent al-Naḍr and ʿUqba to Jewish scholars, who prescribed tests about cave youths, a world-traveling ruler, and the spirit.
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن إسحاق عن ابن عباس بسند، أنه قال: بعثت قريش النضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those claiming God took a child include Jews speaking of ʿUzayr, Christians of the Messiah, and some Arabs of angels.
rows.anchor: أهل هذه المقالة هم بعض اليهود في عزير، والنصارى في المسيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “they have no knowledge of it” may refer to their claim or alleged child; the author objects they are not describing the child.
rows.anchor: والضمير في به يحتمل أن يعود على القول الذي يتضمنه قالوا المتقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers an independent assertion of their ignorance; alternatively the pronoun refers to God, as al-Ṭabarī says, condemning ignorance more strongly.
rows.anchor: والصواب عندي أنه نفي مؤتنف أخبر الله تعالى بجهلهم في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Nor their fathers” means forebears from whom they inherited the claim.
rows.anchor: ولا لآبائهم يريد الذين أخذ هؤلاء هذه المقالة عنهم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read kaburat kalimatan in the accusative; parsed as specification or circumstantial accusative, with “their falsehood” understood.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «كبرت كلمة» بنصب الكلمة

rows.speaker: الحسن ويحيى بن يعمر وابن محيصن والقواس عن ابن كثير
rows.claim: They read kalimatun in the nominative as subject of kaburat.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ويحيى بن يعمر وابن محيصن والقواس عن ابن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A single utterance can be called a “word,” as a poem can; in yaqūlūna means they say only lies.
rows.anchor: وسميت هذه الكلمات كلمة من حيث هي مقالة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse consoles the Prophet; fa-laʿallaka admonishes him not to be so, and bāḵiʿ himself means destroying oneself from grief.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تسلية للنبي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet's phrase al-bāḵiʿ al-wajd nafsahu describes someone destroying himself in grief over what fate removed.
rows.anchor: ألا أيها ذا الباخع الوجد نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “On their tracks” is an eloquent metaphor: people turn from faith and law, leaving the Prophet grieving behind them.
rows.anchor: وقوله على آثارهم، استعارة فصيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This hadith means the Qur'an the Prophet recites; asafan is a verbal noun, and al-Zajjāj defines it as intense grief or anger.
rows.anchor: وقوله بهذا الحديث أي بالقرآن الذي يحدثك به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers grief because the Prophet mourns people beyond his control; anger fits when one has power over its object, as in 43:55; Mujāhid says distress and Qatāda reports anger and grief.
rows.anchor: و «الأسف» في هذا الموضع الحزن، لأنه على من لا يملكه

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā uses asīf to mean sad, like someone whose hand was severed.
rows.anchor: أرى رجلا منكم أسيفا كأنما

rows.speaker: ابن جبير عن ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: They say the earth's adornment means people.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن جبير عن ابن عباس: أراد الرجال وقاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says adornment means caliphs, scholars, and rulers.
rows.anchor: وروى عكرمة عن ابن عباس أن الزينة الخلفاء والعلماء والأمراء

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group says adornment is blessings, clothing, fruits, greenery, and water.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة أراد النعم والملابس والثمار والخضرة والمياه

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group takes earth's adornment generally: all things have beauty through creation and design.
rows.anchor: فرقة: أراد كل ما على الأرض عموما وليس شيء إلا وفيه زينة

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A Prophetic report calls the world lush and sweet, says God makes people successors to test them, and warns about the world and women.
rows.anchor: الدنيا خضرة حلوة وإن الله مستخلفكم فيها فناظر كيف تعملون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zīnata can be the second object of jaʿalnā or its purpose, depending on the verb's meaning.
rows.anchor: وزينة مفعول ثان أو مفعول من أجله بحسب معنى «جعل»

rows.speaker: سفيان الثوري
rows.claim: Sufyān al-Thawrī says the best deeds belong to those most ascetic toward the world.
rows.anchor: قال سفيان الثوري: «أحسنهم عملا» أزهدهم فيها

rows.speaker: أبو عاصم العسقلاني
rows.claim: Abū ʿĀṣim says the best act is to leave the world behind.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عاصم العسقلاني: أحسن عملا: أترك لها

rows.speaker: أبو محمد
rows.claim: The author's father defines good work as taking what is due and spending rightly, with faith, obligations, avoiding prohibitions, and recommended deeds.
rows.anchor: وكان أبي رضي الله عنه يقول: أحسن العمل أخذ بحق واتفاق في حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth's adornment will become barren dust without plants; jurz is empty land, happening region by region now and to all earth at resurrection.
rows.anchor: أي يرجع كل ذلك ترابا غير متزين بنبات ونحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jarazat describes land stripped of vegetation by drought, locusts, or similar causes; arḍūn ajrāz means barren lands.
rows.anchor: يقال: جرزت الأرض بقحط أو جراد أو نحوه إذا ذهب نباتها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj defines jurz as land that does not grow; the author corrects this to land that has not grown.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: والجرز الأرض التي لا تنبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿīd can mean the earth's surface, soil specifically, wholesome earth, or ground raised above a lower area.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وإنما ينبغي أن يقول: التي لم تنبت، و «الصعيد» وجه الأرض

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: For Sībawayh, am without a preceding interrogative alif means “rather” plus an interrogative; others treat it as the interrogative alone.
rows.anchor: مذهب سيبويه في أم إذا جاءت دون أن يتقدمها ألف استفهام

rows.speaker: الطبري وابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: They take the question as rebuke: do not think the cave youths the most amazing sign; other signs are greater.
rows.anchor: فإن سائر آيات الله أعظم من قصتهم وأشنع

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrāwī allows the question to affirm the youths were amazing and prompt the Prophet to describe them, requiring a forced reading of ḥasibta.
rows.anchor: أن تكون استفهاما له هل علم أصحاب الكهف عجبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kahf is a spacious mountain opening, a narrower one a ghār; Anas' reported definition as a mountain is uncommon.
rows.anchor: والكهف النقب المتسع في الجبل وما لم يتسع منها فهو غار

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says al-Raqīm was the village opposite the cave.
rows.anchor: فقال كعب، الرقيم القرية التي كانت بإزاء الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: They identify al-Raqīm as the valley opposite the cave, between ʿUṣbān and Ayla.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وقتادة: الرقيم الوادي الذي كان بإزائه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Other reports call al-Raqīm the mountain containing the cave or a book of the youths' religious law.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا هو الجبل الذي فيه الكهف

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says al-Raqīm was the rock above the cave.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: الرقيم الصخرة التي كانت على الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says al-Raqīm is a book whose matter God concealed and whose story he did not explain.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: كتاب عمى الله علينا أمره ولم يشرح لنا قصته

rows.speaker: فرقة وابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Reports call it a copper or lead tablet inscribed with the youths' story, disappearance, date, and lineage, or a stone tablet at the entrance.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: في لوح رصاص كتب فيه القوم الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accounts suggest early historical record-keeping; the terms derive from inscription, pattern, and a valley bend where water runs.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأقوال مأخوذة من الرقم ومنه كتاب مرقوم

rows.speaker: النقاش عن قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh transmits from Qatāda that al-Raqīm means their money.
rows.anchor:
وقال النقاش عن قتادة:
الرقيم دراهمهم

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك والشعبي
rows.claim: Anas ibn Mālik and al-Shaʿbī say al-Raqīm was the dog.
rows.anchor: وقال أنس بن مالك والشعبي الرقيم الكلب

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says al-Raqīm was an inkwell.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة الرقيم الدواة

rows.speaker: فرقة وابن عباس
rows.claim: Other views say al-Raqīm was another group of youths in al-Sarāt, or Ibn ʿAbbās did not know whether it was a book or structure; a report lists words he did not know.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: الرقيم كان لفتية آخرين في السراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We do not waste the reward” is an emphatic parenthesis recalling God's favor between believers and promised gardens.
rows.anchor: اعتراض مؤكد للمعنى، مذكر بأفضال الله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj allows the clause to predicate inna, since good-doers are believers whose reward is not wasted.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: ويجوز أن يكون خبر إن في قوله إنا لا نضيع

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh parses “we do not waste” as predicate with omitted return pronoun “among them.”
rows.anchor: ومذهب سيبويه أن الخبر في قوله لا نضيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAdn means residence, like a mineral deposit whose stone remains in place; “beneath them” means beneath their rooms and buildings.
rows.anchor: و «العدن» : الإقامة، ومنه المعدن، لأن حجره مقيم فيه ثابت

rows.speaker: الجمهور وأبان عن عاصم
rows.claim: The majority read asāwir; Abān from ʿĀṣim reads aswira without alif and extra hāʾ; both denote forearm bracelets.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «من أساور» وروى أبان عن عاصم «أسورة»

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة معمر
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says asāwir may be plural of iswār or of uswara, plural of siwār; one form means Persian leader, another bracelet.
rows.anchor: وقيل أساور جمع أسورة، وأسورة جمع سوار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rajaz poem cited by Ibn al-Anbārī uses aswār for a feared ruler at whose gate the speaker might beg.
rows.anchor: أو لاضم ليس له أسوار ... لما رآني ملك جبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sundus is fine brocade, istabraq thick; some call the latter arabized foreign, others derive it from Arabic.
rows.anchor: و «السندس» : رقيق الديباج، و «الإستبرق» ما غلظ منه

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads istabraq with connected hamza; al-Ahwāzī transmits it and Abū al-Fatḥ calls it error or near-error.
rows.anchor: أن ابن محيصن قرأ «من سندس وإستبرق» فجاء موصول الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arāʾik are beds in chambers; “beautiful” refers to gardens.
rows.anchor: والأرائك جمع أريكة هي السرير في المجال

rows.speaker: أبو عمران الجوني
rows.claim: Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī says istabraq is silk woven with gold.
rows.anchor: أنه قال: «الإستبرق» الحرير المنسوج بالذهب

rows.speaker: مكي والزهراوي
rows.claim: A report says these verses were revealed about Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and ʿAlī, present when the Prophet answered a Bedouin.
rows.anchor: نزلت في أبي بكر وعمر وعثمان وعلي رضي الله عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable addresses the arrogant group seeking to dismiss poor believers and those believers; owners represent a Qurayshi/Tamīmī notable and Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, and peers.
rows.anchor: الضمير في لهم عائد على الطائفة المتجبرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaffafnāhumā means palms surrounded the gardens on every side; ḥifāf can mean a couch or furrow's side.
rows.anchor: وحففناهما بمعنى وجعلنا ذلك لها من كل جهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable seems actual, as most interpreters hold, though hypothetical is possible; the author prefers historicity.
rows.anchor: وظاهر هذا المثل أنه بأمر وقع وكان موجودا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says Israelite brothers inherited four thousand dinars; one invested in wealth while the other spent in obedience and became poor, then the rich brother boasted.
rows.anchor: وروي في ذلك أنهما كانا أخوين من بني إسرائيل، ورثا أربعة آلاف دينار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says they were blacksmith partners who amassed money and followed contrasting paths.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهما كانا شريكين حدادين، كسبا مالا كثيرا

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن القاسم الكاتب
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Qāsim says the gardens were at Lake Tinnīs; one brother sold his share, spent the proceeds in obedience, and they drowned in one night. The author omits unreliable stories.
rows.anchor: وفي بسط قصصهما طول فاختصرته واقتصرت على معناه لقلة صحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scene is a productive estate of vines, palms, grain, and a stream, reducing labor and water-lifting.
rows.anchor: جنتا عنب أحاط بهما نخل، بينهما فسحة، هي مزدرع لجميع الحبوب

rows.speaker: الجمهور وعبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: The majority read kiltā; ʿAbd Allāh's codex reads kilā. Sībawayh derives tāʾ from wāw; either means each of two.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «كلتا» ، وفي مصحف عبد الله «كلا»

rows.speaker: الفراء وابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ cites Ibn Masʿūd's reading kull al-jannatayni ātā aklahu; akl means edible fruit.
rows.anchor: و «الأكل» ثمرها الذي يؤكل منها، قال الفراء: وفي قراءة ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It did not diminish anything” means neither garden fell short of its fullest normal yield.
rows.anchor: أي لم تنقص عن العرف الأتم الذي يشبه فيها

rows.speaker: الجمهور وسلام ويعقوب وعيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: The majority read fajjarnā with doubled jīm; Salām, Yaʿqūb, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read single jīm and fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «وفجرنا» بشد الجيم

rows.speaker: الجمهور وأبو السمال والفياض بن غزوان وطلحة بن سليمان
rows.claim: The majority read nahran with fatḥa on hāʾ; Abū al-Sammāl, al-Fayyāḍ, and Ṭalḥa use sukūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «نهرا» بفتح الهاء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: They read thamar with ḍamma on both letters as plural of thimār; others use mīm sukūn as lightening, perhaps plural of thamarah.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وابن عباس ومجاهد

rows.speaker: عاصم وأبو جعفر والحسن وجابر بن زيد والحجاج
rows.claim: They read thamar with fatḥa on both letters, meaning tree fruit.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم «ثمر» وبثمره يفتح الميم والثاء فيهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: They take thumur as all wealth including gold, silver, and livestock; they cite al-Nābigha.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس وقتادة: «الثمر» جميع المال من الذهب والفضة والحيوان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid restricts thumur to gold and silver.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد يراد بها الذهب والفضة خاصة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says thumur means the rootstock that bears fruit.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد «الثمر» هي الأصول التي فيها الثمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa, thamar means fruit; mentioning fruit economically implies destruction of roots supplying future yields.
rows.anchor: فلا إشكال في أن المعنى ما في رؤوس الشجر من الأكل

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy's codex says God gave him abundant fruit or wealth.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أبي «وآتيناه ثمرا كثيرا»

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abū Rajāʾ reads thamar with fatḥa on thāʾ and sukūn on mīm.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء «وكان له ثمر» بفتح الثاء وسكون الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muḥāwara means exchange of speech and derives from ḥāra-yaḥūru.
rows.anchor: والمحاورة مراجعة القول، وهو من حار يحور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some infer “more men” means the pair were not brothers; the reply says nafar means servants who fulfill his needs.
rows.anchor: واستدل بعض الناس من قوله وأعز نفرا على أنه لم يكن أخاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boast displays arrogance and parallels ʿUyayna and al-Aqraʿ telling the Prophet to dismiss Salmān and companions.
rows.anchor: فنح عنا سلمان وقرناءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author derives fiʾa from fāʾa-yafīʾu, dropping middle radical for ease; Abū ʿAlī derives fāwata, morphologically better but weaker in meaning.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهي عندي من فاء يفيء وزنها فئة

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads fiʾatan tanṣuruhu with accusative fiʾatan.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة: «فئة تنصره»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hunalika may modify muntaṣiran, or al-wilāya may be subject with hunālika as predicate.
rows.anchor: وقوله هنالك يحتمل أن يكون ظرفا لقوله منتصرا

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي والأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: They read al-wilāya with kasra on wāw, meaning sovereignty or leadership.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي والأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب «الولاية» بكسر الواو

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: Other readers use fatḥa on wāw, meaning alliance and connection.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون «الولاية» بفتح الواو وهي بمعنى الموالاة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو والأصمعي
rows.claim: They call kasra incorrect because the pattern marks a craft or assumed state, not alliance.
rows.anchor: ويحكى عن أبي عمرو والأصمعي أن كسر الواو هنا لحن

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو والكسائي
rows.claim: They read al-ḥaqq nominative as adjective of al-wilāya.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو والكسائي «الحق» بالرفع على جهة النعت

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: Other readers put al-ḥaqq genitive as adjective of God.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون «الحق» بالخفض على النعت لله عز وجل

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywa reads “to God, the Real” with al-ḥaqq accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة «لله الحق» بالنصب

rows.speaker: الجمهور وعاصم وحمزة والحسن
rows.claim: The majority read ʿuqban with ḍamma on both letters; other readings use still qāf or feminine ʿuqbā, all meaning outcome.
rows.anchor: والعقب والعقب بمعنى العاقبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير وأبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل
rows.claim: They identify enduring righteous deeds as the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس وابن جبير وأبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل: هي الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority identify them as formulas of glorification, praise, unity, greatness, and reliance; reports urge frequent recitation.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور هي الكلمات المأثور فضلها: سبحان الله والحمد الله ولا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another view defines them as every good word or deed preserved for the afterlife; al-Ṭabarī prefers it and author says Ibn ʿAbbās' views indicate generality.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا الباقيات الصالحات: كل عمل صالح من قول أو فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their doer has better reward and hope than one with wealth and children but no righteous work.
rows.anchor: صاحبها ينتظر الثواب وينبسط على خير من حال ذي المال والبنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means “remember the day when We move the mountains,” the most eloquent construal here.
rows.anchor: التقدير: واذكر يوم، وهذا أفصح ما يتأول في هذا هنا

rows.speaker: نافع والأعرج وشيبة وعاصم وابن مصرف وأبو عبد الرحمن
rows.claim: They read nusayyiru; others read tusayyiru, yusayyiru, tasīru, or Ubayy's “when mountains were moved.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع والأعرج وشيبة وعاصم وابن مصرف وأبو عبد الرحمن «نسير»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bare earth may mean mountains, hills, and trees vanished, or its inhabitants emerged into view.
rows.anchor: وقوله بارزة إما أن يريد أن الأرض، لذهاب الجبال والظراب والشجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We gathered them” means raising people from graves and assembling them for the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وحشرناهم أي أقمناهم من قبورهم، وجعلناهم لعرضة القيامة

rows.speaker: الجمهور وقتادة وأبان بن يزيد عن عاصم والضحاك
rows.claim: The majority read nughādir; Qatāda reads tugādir, Abān from ʿĀṣim yugādir with nominative aḥad, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk naghdir.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «نغادر» بنون العظمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-kitāb may be each person's angel-record or one single book placed before them.
rows.anchor: الكتاب اسم جنس، يراد به كتب الناس التي أحصاها الحفظة لواحد واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Criminals fear exposure; their complaint concerns complete accounting, not injustice. Lesser deeds come first to emphasize them and imply greater deeds are more surely recorded.
rows.anchor: و «إشفاق المجرمين» : فزعهم من كشفه لهم وفضحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs often name the lesser of paired things first, as in al-qamarān and al-ʿumarān.
rows.anchor: والعرب أبدا تقدم في الذكر الأقل من كل مقترنين
